critical_code_review_comments: server.py is now 1061 lines (was 951 in iter3). Still a single-file backend — auth (Google + JWT + reset + brute force + refresh rotation + add/change password + security state), public content, patient CRUD, labs, messaging, doctor notes, admin, AI, and seed are all in one module. Please split into routers.

In /auth/refresh, when the presented jti is not active (reuse detected), the server correctly mass-revokes but does NOT log the incident. Reuse-detection is a security event; a WARN log line 'refresh token reuse detected for user_id=... jti=...' would be valuable for forensics.

/auth/add-password sets a password without any confirmation step or email verification. If a stale Google session cookie is compromised (e.g. XSS on a shared machine), the attacker can attach a persistent password. Consider requiring the Google session to have been created within the last N minutes, or send a confirmation email before enabling password auth.

/auth/security uses `has_google = bool(full.get('picture'))` as a proxy for 'user has a Google auth method'. A patient may have a picture set through some future non-Google flow. Prefer explicit tracking: e.g. an `auth_providers: ['google']` array on the user document.

Cleaning up refresh_sessions relies solely on hitting /auth/refresh or /auth/logout. Expired refresh tokens accumulate in the collection forever because there's no TTL index. Add a TTL index on `expires_at` (or store it as a native datetime + createIndex expireAfterSeconds=0).

clear_auth_cookies in /auth/refresh reuse-detection path clears cookies using response.delete_cookie without samesite='none'; secure=True — same footgun as before (some browsers won't accept the clear across-site).

get_current_user still silently swallows both ExpiredSignatureError and InvalidTokenError on the JWT path and falls back to session_token. An expired access_token should return a distinguishable signal so the frontend calls /auth/refresh instead of masquerading as unauthenticated.
AddPasswordRequest uses `min_length=8` but there's no server-side password strength check (no digit/special char requirement). Consider a shared password policy.

/auth/add-password does not require the client to prove the Google session is fresh (e.g. via re-authenticate). Standard practice for security-sensitive setting changes is to require a fresh authentication (last N minutes).
